cls: Trace element / mineral - intestinal copper-absorption inhibitor (maintenance therapy for Wilson disease)
quick: Wilson disease: 50 mg elemental zinc orally three times daily
Take on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2-3 hours after food
Used in Wilson disease when needed; benefits weighed against risk
Zinc passes into milk; use with caution
No specific adjustment at usual doses
Used in Wilson disease (hepatic copper overload) under monitoring
Urinary copper, serum zinc/copper, LFTs (Wilson disease)
summary: Zinc acetate is an oral zinc salt used as maintenance therapy in Wilson disease, where it blocks intestinal absorption of copper, and as a source of supplemental zinc. In Wilson disease it induces intestinal metallothionein, which binds dietary and endogenous copper and prevents its absorption, promoting faecal copper loss. It is generally well tolerated, with gastric upset being the main adverse effect, and is taken on an empty stomach for full effect.
indications: Maintenance treatment of Wilson disease (after initial chelation therapy)
Treatment and prevention of zinc deficiency

dosage.n: Total 150 mg/day elemental zinc; take between meals
Dose by age/weight per specialist guidance

admin: Take on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2-3 hours after meals, for best absorption and copper-blocking effect
If gastric upset occurs, the first dose may be taken with a little protein (e.g., between meals with a small amount of food), accepting some loss of efficacy
Separate from iron, calcium and other mineral supplements which compete for absorption
In Wilson disease, continue lifelong maintenance and avoid high-copper foods
moa: Zinc induces synthesis of metallothionein in intestinal mucosal cells. Metallothionein has a high binding affinity for copper, sequestering both dietary copper and endogenous copper re-secreted into the gut. The bound copper is then lost as intestinal cells are shed into the stool, producing a negative copper balance. This non-toxic mechanism prevents copper accumulation in Wilson disease.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to zinc salts or excipients
relative: Conditions worsened by reduced copper (e.g., neutropenia, sideroblastic anemia)

preg: In Wilson disease, treatment must continue during pregnancy because uncontrolled copper accumulation is harmful; zinc is often preferred and given at a reduced dose with close monitoring. For routine supplementation, recommended dietary intakes are appropriate.
lact: Zinc is excreted into breast milk. Use cautiously during breastfeeding; in Wilson disease, monitor the infant and balance maternal need against potential infant zinc exposure.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is required at usual therapeutic or supplemental doses.
hepatic: Zinc is used specifically in Wilson disease, a disorder of hepatic copper overload; hepatic function and copper indices should be monitored. No routine dose reduction is required for hepatic impairment per se.

moderate: Copper (zinc reduces copper absorption - the basis of Wilson disease therapy, but can cause deficiency)
Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones (zinc chelates them, reducing antibiotic absorption - separate doses)
Penicillamine and other chelators (reduce zinc absorption; separate from zinc dosing)
minor: Iron and calcium supplements (compete for absorption)
interactions.food: Food, especially phytates and dairy, reduces zinc absorption - take on an empty stomach
interactions.diagnostics: Affects serum/urinary copper and zinc levels used for monitoring

serious: Copper deficiency with anemia and neutropenia (over-treatment)
emergency: Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis from copper deficiency (with prolonged over-treatment)

monitoring: 24-hour urinary copper excretion to assess adequacy in Wilson disease
Serum zinc levels and urinary zinc for adherence
Complete blood count for copper-deficiency anemia/neutropenia
counsel: Take on an empty stomach for best effect, away from food and other mineral supplements
If it upsets your stomach, you may take it with a small amount of protein, but tell your doctor
In Wilson disease this is lifelong therapy - do not stop without specialist advice
Avoid copper-rich foods (liver, shellfish, chocolate, nuts) as advised
Report unusual tiredness, frequent infections, or easy bruising (possible copper deficiency)
pk: Copper-blocking effect develops over days to weeks (metallothionein induction)
Serum zinc peaks within ~2-4 hours of an oral dose
Biological half-life of zinc in tissues is prolonged (days)
Sustained anti-copper effect requires consistent multiple daily dosing
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture
pearls: Zinc acetate (Galzin) is a maintenance therapy for Wilson disease; it is not used as initial de-coppering in symptomatic patients, where chelators act faster
Mechanism is induction of intestinal metallothionein, which traps copper and sheds it in stool
Must be taken on an empty stomach, separated from food and mineral supplements, for efficacy
Over-treatment can cause copper deficiency with anemia and neutropenia - monitor copper status
Zinc chelates tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics - separate administration by several hours
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double up. In Wilson disease, consistent dosing is important; report repeated missed doses to your specialist.
overdose: Acute zinc overdose causes nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea; very large ingestions can cause more serious gastrointestinal and systemic effects. Chronic excess leads to copper deficiency (anemia, neutropenia). Management is supportive; for massive acute ingestion, chelation may be considered. Treat copper deficiency by reducing zinc and supplementing copper.
